claim: In the fission yeast Schizosaccharomyces pombe, a YTH family RNA-binding protein, Mmi1, directs the nuclear exosome-mediated elimination of meiotic transcripts during vegetative proliferation.
source: In the fission yeast Schizosaccharomyces pombe, a YTH family RNA-binding protein, Mmi1, directs the nuclear exosome-mediated elimination of meiotic transcripts during vegetative proliferation.
evidence: This is a well-established finding in the field, supported by prior research and presented as background information.

claim: Mmi1 induces the formation of facultative heterochromatin at a subset of its target genes.
source: Mmi1 also induces the formation of facultative heterochromatin at a subset of its target genes.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract and introduction.

claim: Mmi1 prevents the mistimed expression of meiotic proteins by tethering their mRNAs to the nuclear foci.
source: Here, we show that Mmi1 prevents the mistimed expression of meiotic proteins by tethering their mRNAs to the nuclear foci.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in multiple figures.

claim: Mmi1 interacts with itself with the assistance of a homolog of Enhancer of Rudimentary, Erh1.
source: Mmi1 interacts with itself with the assistance of a homolog of Enhancer of Rudimentary, Erh1.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunoprecipitation and two-hybrid data shown in Figures 4 and 6.

claim: Mmi1 self-interaction is required for foci formation, target transcript elimination, their nuclear retention, and protein expression inhibition.
source: Mmi1 self-interaction is required for foci formation, target transcript elimination, their nuclear retention, and protein expression inhibition.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experiments with Mmi1 deletion mutants shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Nuclear foci formed by Mmi1 are not only the site of RNA degradation, but also of sequestration of meiotic transcripts from the translation machinery.
source: We propose that nuclear foci formed by Mmi1 are not only the site of RNA degradation, but also of sequestration of meiotic transcripts from the translation machinery.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by data showing nuclear retention of transcripts and prevention of protein expression.

claim: Ectopic expression of germline genes causes various cellular defects, including genome instability and tumorigenesis.
source: It has been demonstrated that ectopic expression of germline genes causes various cellular defects, including genome instability and tumorigenesis (Folco et al., 2017; Greve et al., 2015; Janic et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Hundreds of genes are upregulated when the fission yeast Schizosaccharomyces pombe cells enter meiosis from the mitotic cell cycle in response to nutrient starvation.
source: Hundreds of genes are upregulated when the fission yeast Schizosaccharomyces pombe cells enter meiosis from the mitotic cell cycle in response to nutrient starvation (Mata et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: During the mitotic cell cycle, meiotic genes are strictly suppressed by post-transcriptional mechanisms, in addition to transcriptional regulation.
source: During the mitotic cell cycle, meiotic genes are strictly suppressed by post-transcriptional mechanisms, in addition to transcriptional regulation, since mistimed expression of meiotic genes severely impairs cell growth.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Mistimed expression of meiotic genes severely impairs cell growth.
source: During the mitotic cell cycle, meiotic genes are strictly suppressed by post-transcriptional mechanisms, in addition to transcriptional regulation, since mistimed expression of meiotic genes severely impairs cell growth.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and is consistent with the experimental observations in the manuscript.

claim: A large number of meiosis-specific transcripts carry a specific region called DSR (determinant of selective removal) and are recognized by a YTH family RNA-binding protein, Mmi1, in mitotically growing S. pombe cells.
source: A large number of meiosis-specific transcripts carry a specific region called DSR (determinant of selective removal) and are recognized by a YTH family RNA-binding protein, Mmi1, in mitotically growing S. pombe cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by prior research.

claim: Mmi1 induces nuclear exosome-mediated RNA elimination.
source: Mmi1 then induces nuclear exosome-mediated RNA elimination (Harigaya et al., 2006; Yamanaka et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: DSR activity is exhibited by enriched repeats of the hexanucleotide UNAAAC motif.
source: DSR activity is exhibited by enriched repeats of the hexanucleotide UNAAAC motif (Hiriart et al., 2012; Yamashita et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The Mmi1 YTH domain preferentially binds to the unmethylated UNAAAC motif.
source: The Mmi1 YTH domain preferentially binds to the unmethylated UNAAAC motif, contrasting with the YTH domains in other organisms including mammals, which selectively bind to N6-methyladenosine-containing RNAs (Chatterjee et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2016; Wu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: YTH domains in other organisms including mammals selectively bind to N6-methyladenosine-containing RNAs.
source: The Mmi1 YTH domain preferentially binds to the unmethylated UNAAAC motif, contrasting with the YTH domains in other organisms including mammals, which selectively bind to N6-methyladenosine-containing RNAs (Chatterjee et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2016; Wu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The DSR region has been found in a group of meiotic transcripts including mei4, which encodes a key meiotic transcription factor.
source: The DSR region has been found in a group of meiotic transcripts including mei4, which encodes a key meiotic transcription factor (Horie et al., 1998), and ssm4, which encodes a subunit of the dynactin complex (Niccoli et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: ssm4 encodes a subunit of the dynactin complex.
source: The DSR region has been found in a group of meiotic transcripts including mei4, which encodes a key meiotic transcription factor (Horie et al., 1998), and ssm4, which encodes a subunit of the dynactin complex (Niccoli et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Red1, a zinc-finger protein, is another crucial factor involved in the Mmi1-driven RNA elimination.
source: Red1, a zinc-finger protein, is another crucial factor involved in the Mmi1-driven RNA elimination (Sugiyama and Sugioka-Sugiyama, 2011; Yamashita et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Red1 constitutes a complex termed MTREC (Mtl1-Red1 core) or NURS (nuclear RNA silencing) with the Mtr4-like RNA helicase, Mtl1.
source: Red1 constitutes a complex termed MTREC (Mtl1-Red1 core) or NURS (nuclear RNA silencing) with the Mtr4-like RNA helicase, Mtl1, and transfers the Mmi1-bound meiotic transcripts to the nuclear exosome (Egan et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Red1 transfers the Mmi1-bound meiotic transcripts to the nuclear exosome.
source: Red1 constitutes a complex termed MTREC (Mtl1-Red1 core) or NURS (nuclear RNA silencing) with the Mtr4-like RNA helicase, Mtl1, and transfers the Mmi1-bound meiotic transcripts to the nuclear exosome (Egan et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In human cells, a similar protein complex, PAXT, composed of a Red1-related zinc-finger protein (ZFC3H1) and an Mtr4 ortholog (hMTR4), has been reported to induce nuclear exosome-dependent RNA degradation.
source: In human cells, a similar protein complex, PAXT, composed of a Red1-related zinc-finger protein (ZFC3H1) and an Mtr4 ortholog (hMTR4), has been reported to induce nuclear exosome-dependent RNA degradation (Meola et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: ZFC3H1 and hMtr4 prevent nuclear export of non-coding RNAs.
source: Recently, ZFC3H1 and hMtr4 have also been shown to prevent nuclear export of non-coding RNAs (Ogami et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Mmi1 forms several dot structures in the nucleus of the mitotically growing cells.
source: Mmi1 forms several dot structures in the nucleus of the mitotically growing cells (Harigaya et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Many factors cooperating with Mmi1, including Red1 and exosome subunits, localize to the Mmi1 foci.
source: Many factors cooperating with Mmi1, including Red1 and exosome subunits, localize to the Mmi1 foci (Sugiyama and Sugioka-Sugiyama, 2011; Yamanaka et al., 2010; Yamashita et al., 2013), suggesting that the foci are the site of degradation of the DSR-containing meiotic transcripts; however, the precise location of the Mmi1 foci in the nucleus remains elusive.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The Mmi1 foci are the site of degradation of the DSR-containing meiotic transcripts.
source: Many factors cooperating with Mmi1, including Red1 and exosome subunits, localize to the Mmi1 foci (Sugiyama and Sugioka-Sugiyama, 2011; Yamanaka et al., 2010; Yamashita et al., 2013), suggesting that the foci are the site of degradation of the DSR-containing meiotic transcripts; however, the precise location of the Mmi1 foci in the nucleus remains elusive.
evidence: This is presented as a suggestion based on prior research, with acknowledgment that the precise location remains unclear.

claim: The precise location of the Mmi1 foci in the nucleus remains elusive.
source: Many factors cooperating with Mmi1, including Red1 and exosome subunits, localize to the Mmi1 foci (Sugiyama and Sugioka-Sugiyama, 2011; Yamanaka et al., 2010; Yamashita et al., 2013), suggesting that the foci are the site of degradation of the DSR-containing meiotic transcripts; however, the precise location of the Mmi1 foci in the nucleus remains elusive.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in current knowledge.

claim: When S. pombe cells initiate meiosis, Mmi1-mediated RNA degradation must be suppressed so that DSR-containing meiotic transcripts are expressed.
source: When S. pombe cells initiate meiosis, Mmi1-mediated RNA degradation must be suppressed so that DSR-containing meiotic transcripts are expressed.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Downregulation of Mmi1 during meiosis is achieved by sequestration of Mmi1 to a meiosis-specific chromosome-associated dot, Mei2 dot.
source: Downregulation of Mmi1 during meiosis is achieved by sequestration of Mmi1 to a meiosis-specific chromosome-associated dot, Mei2 dot (Harigaya et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Mei2 dot is composed of an RNA-binding protein, Mei2, and its binding partner, meiRNA, and is located at the sme2 locus, which encodes meiRNA.
source: Mei2 dot is composed of an RNA-binding protein, Mei2, and its binding partner, meiRNA, and is located at the sme2 locus, which encodes meiRNA (Shimada et al., 2003; Watanabe et al., 1997; Yamashita et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: meiRNA carries the DSR region and is targeted by Mmi1.
source: meiRNA carries the DSR region and is targeted by Mmi1, suggesting that meiRNA serves as a decoy for luring Mmi1 (Shichino et al., 2014; Yamashita et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: meiRNA serves as a decoy for luring Mmi1.
source: meiRNA carries the DSR region and is targeted by Mmi1, suggesting that meiRNA serves as a decoy for luring Mmi1 (Shichino et al., 2014; Yamashita et al., 2012).
evidence: This is presented as a suggestion based on prior research.

claim: Binding of Mmi1 to target transcripts triggers the recruitment of factors involved in heterochromatin formation along with Red1.
source: Binding of Mmi1 to target transcripts triggers the recruitment of factors involved in heterochromatin formation along with Red1.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: A highly conserved multiprotein complex, Ccr4/Not, participates in the Mmi1-mediated heterochromatin formation, albeit to a limited extent.
source: It has been demonstrated that a highly conserved multiprotein complex, Ccr4/Not, participates in the Mmi1-mediated heterochromatin formation, albeit to a limited extent (Cotobal et al., 2015; Sugiyama et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Mmi1 accelerates deadenylation by Ccr4/Not.
source: Mmi1 has also been shown to accelerate deadenylation by Ccr4/Not, although its in vivo significance remains unknown (Stowell et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research, with acknowledgment that in vivo significance is unclear.

claim: The in vivo significance of Mmi1-mediated acceleration of deadenylation by Ccr4/Not remains unknown.
source: Mmi1 has also been shown to accelerate deadenylation by Ccr4/Not, although its in vivo significance remains unknown (Stowell et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as a gap in current knowledge.

claim: Mmi1 regulates the termination of transcription of its target genes.
source: Furthermore, Mmi1 regulates the termination of transcription of its target genes (Chalamcharla et al., 2015; Shah et al., 2014; Touat-Todeschini et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Mmi1-mediated termination of an upstream non-coding RNA ensures the expression of downstream genes.
source: Our recent study has revealed that Mmi1-mediated termination of an upstream non-coding RNA ensures the expression of downstream genes (Touat-Todeschini et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research by the authors.

claim: Disruption of mmi1 results in a severe growth defect due to the aberrant expression of meiotic transcripts.
source: Disruption of mmi1 results in a severe growth defect due to the aberrant expression of meiotic transcripts.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: The growth defect caused by disruption of mmi1 was alleviated by the deletion of mei4.
source: This defect was alleviated by the deletion of mei4 (Harigaya et al., 2006), indicating that mei4 is a crucial target of Mmi1-mediated elimination.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: mei4 is a crucial target of Mmi1-mediated elimination.
source: This defect was alleviated by the deletion of mei4 (Harigaya et al., 2006), indicating that mei4 is a crucial target of Mmi1-mediated elimination.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that mei4 deletion alleviates the mmi1 disruption phenotype.

claim: red1∆ cells inappropriately accumulate meiotic transcripts such as mei4 and ssm4 during vegetative growth.
source: red1∆ cells inappropriately accumulate meiotic transcripts such as mei4 and ssm4 during vegetative growth, but are viable albeit showing cold and weak high-temperature sensitivity (Figure 1A,B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B) (Sugiyama and Sugioka-Sugiyama, 2011; Yamashita et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in figures and citations to prior research.

claim: red1∆ cells are viable albeit showing cold and weak high-temperature sensitivity.
source: red1∆ cells inappropriately accumulate meiotic transcripts such as mei4 and ssm4 during vegetative growth, but are viable albeit showing cold and weak high-temperature sensitivity (Figure 1A,B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B) (Sugiyama and Sugioka-Sugiyama, 2011; Yamashita et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1A and citations to prior research.

claim: Deletion of mei4 did not suppress the temperature-sensitivity of red1∆ cells.
source: Deletion of mei4 did not suppress this temperature-sensitivity (Figure 1A), suggesting that these defects are independent of meiotic transcript accumulation.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The temperature-sensitivity defects of red1∆ cells are independent of meiotic transcript accumulation.
source: Deletion of mei4 did not suppress this temperature-sensitivity (Figure 1A), suggesting that these defects are independent of meiotic transcript accumulation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that mei4 deletion does not suppress the temperature sensitivity.

claim: A temperature-sensitive mutant of rrp6 shows temperature-sensitivity similar to red1∆ cells.
source: This was also the case in a temperature-sensitive mutant of rrp6, which encodes a catalytic subunit of the nuclear exosome (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: rrp6 encodes a catalytic subunit of the nuclear exosome.
source: This was also the case in a temperature-sensitive mutant of rrp6, which encodes a catalytic subunit of the nuclear exosome (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: mei4 transcripts were ectopically accumulated in both mmi1-ts3 and red1∆ mutants during the mitotic cell cycle.
source: mei4 transcripts were ectopically accumulated in both mutants during the mitotic cell cycle (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Mei4 protein expression was hardly detected in red1∆ cells, but accumulated in cells with reduced Mmi1 activity.
source: Strikingly, Mei4 protein expression was hardly detected in red1∆ cells, but accumulated in cells with reduced Mmi1 activity (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: In the temperature-sensitive rrp6-32 mutant, expression of Mei4 protein was suppressed, whereas mei4 transcripts accumulated.
source: In the temperature-sensitive rrp6-32 mutant, expression of Mei4 protein was suppressed, whereas mei4 transcripts accumulated, as seen in red1∆ cells (Figure 1B,C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B, 1C, and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Mei4 protein was detected in both mmi1-ts3 red1∆ and mmi1-ts3 rrp6-32 double mutants.
source: Mei4 protein was detected in both mmi1-ts3 red1∆ and mmi1-ts3 rrp6-32 double mutants, indicating that Mei4 protein expression requires both transcript accumulation and Mmi1 inactivation.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Mei4 protein expression requires both transcript accumulation and Mmi1 inactivation.
source: Mei4 protein was detected in both mmi1-ts3 red1∆ and mmi1-ts3 rrp6-32 double mutants, indicating that Mei4 protein expression requires both transcript accumulation and Mmi1 inactivation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Mei4 protein is only detected when both conditions are met.

claim: Protein expression of ssm4 was detected when Mmi1 activity was dampened.
source: Similarly, protein expression of ssm4, another DSR-containing gene, was detected when Mmi1 activity was dampened (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Mmi1 likely inhibits the expression of proteins encoded by ectopically accumulated DSR-containing mRNAs.
source: These results suggest that Mmi1 likely inhibits the expression of proteins encoded by ectopically accumulated DSR-containing mRNAs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations showing that protein expression is suppressed when Mmi1 is active, even when transcripts accumulate.

claim: mei4 and ssm4 transcripts were concentrated in the nucleus in red1∆ or rrp6-32 cells.
source: We detected a concentration of mei4 and ssm4 transcripts in the nucleus in red1∆ or rrp6-32 cells (Figure 2A,B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by smFISH data shown in Figure 2A, 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, 1B.

claim: In red1∆ and rrp6-32 cells, most nuclear RNA spots were larger than cytoplasmic spots, suggesting that multiple molecules of mei4 or ssm4 transcripts could have converged in the nucleus.
source: In red1∆ and rrp6-32 cells, most nuclear RNA spots were larger than cytoplasmic spots, suggesting that multiple molecules of mei4 or ssm4 transcripts could have converged in the nucleus.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of larger nuclear spots in the smFISH data.

claim: When the Mmi1 function was compromised, mei4 and ssm4 transcripts were exported from the nucleus.
source: In contrast, when the Mmi1 function was compromised, these transcripts were exported from the nucleus.
evidence: This is supported by smFISH data shown in Figure 2A, 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, 1B.

claim: Mmi1 impedes the translation of DSR-containing meiotic transcripts by retaining them in the nucleus.
source: These observations support the idea that Mmi1 impedes the translation of DSR-containing meiotic transcripts by retaining them in the nucleus.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that transcripts are retained in the nucleus when Mmi1 is active and exported when Mmi1 is compromised.

claim: The cytoplasmic distribution of mei4 and ssm4 transcripts in mmi1 mutant cells was halted by the inactivation of Rae1.
source: The cytoplasmic distribution of mei4 and ssm4 transcripts in mmi1 mutant cells was halted by the inactivation of Rae1 (Figure 2C,D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D), which is an essential factor in the nuclear export of mRNAs (Brown et al., 1995; Yoon et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by smFISH data shown in Figure 2C, 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, 1D.

claim: Rae1 is an essential factor in the nuclear export of mRNAs.
source: The cytoplasmic distribution of mei4 and ssm4 transcripts in mmi1 mutant cells was halted by the inactivation of Rae1 (Figure 2C,D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D), which is an essential factor in the nuclear export of mRNAs (Brown et al., 1995; Yoon et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The nuclear export of DSR transcripts is mediated by the canonical mRNA export pathway.
source: This suggests that the nuclear export of DSR transcripts is mediated by the canonical mRNA export pathway.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Rae1 inactivation prevents export of DSR transcripts.

claim: Elevation of mei4 and ssm4 transcript levels was observed in rae1-167 cells.
source: Elevation of mei4 and ssm4 transcript levels was observed in rae1-167 cells, as shown previously (Sugiyama et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Transcripts carrying eight and more DSR motifs in the reporter system were degraded and decay fragments containing U1A tag were observed.
source: Transcripts carrying eight and more DSR motifs in our reporter system were degraded and decay fragments containing U1A tag were observed, whereas transcripts carrying four motifs were stably expressed (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Transcripts carrying four DSR motifs were stably expressed.
source: Transcripts carrying eight and more DSR motifs in our reporter system were degraded and decay fragments containing U1A tag were observed, whereas transcripts carrying four motifs were stably expressed (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Foci were detected in mitotic cells expressing the reporter constructs with eight and more DSR motifs.
source: We detected foci in mitotic cells expressing the reporter constructs with eight and more DSR motifs (Figure 3B,C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3B, 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The observed foci may have formed from the degraded fragments of reporter transcripts carrying U1A tag.
source: These findings indicate that the observed foci may have formed from the degraded fragments of reporter transcripts carrying U1A tag.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that foci are detected when transcripts are degraded.

claim: Foci formation took place inside the nucleus.
source: Foci formation took place inside the nucleus, confirmed by simultaneous observation of the nucleoporin Nup60 (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Foci were scarcely observed in cells expressing transcripts containing 0 and 4 DSR motifs.
source: Foci were scarcely observed in cells expressing transcripts containing 0 and 4 DSR motifs, suggesting that, unlike smFISH, transcripts could be detected in this system only when a certain concentration of molecules were gathered.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3B, 3C.

claim: Transcripts could be detected in the U1A-YFP reporter system only when a certain concentration of molecules were gathered.
source: Foci were scarcely observed in cells expressing transcripts containing 0 and 4 DSR motifs, suggesting that, unlike smFISH, transcripts could be detected in this system only when a certain concentration of molecules were gathered.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that foci are only detected with higher numbers of DSR motifs.

claim: The frequency of cells exhibiting foci and the number of foci per cell increased with the number of DSR motifs.
source: The frequency of cells exhibiting foci and the number of foci per cell increased with the number of DSR motifs (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: DSR-transcript foci coincided with Mmi1.
source: DSR-transcript foci coincided with Mmi1 (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by colocalization data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Foci formation was severely impaired in mmi1∆ cells, although the transcripts escaped degradation and accumulated.
source: Foci formation was severely impaired in mmi1∆ cells, although the transcripts escaped degradation and accumulated (Figure 3F,G and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,B,C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3F, 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A, 2B, 2C.

claim: DSR transcripts were dispersed in the absence of Mmi1.
source: These observations suggest that DSR transcripts were dispersed in the absence of Mmi1.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that foci formation is impaired in mmi1∆ cells.

claim: In red1∆ and rrp6-32 cells, in which degradation of DSR transcripts was compromised, foci became prominent, and the frequencies of cells carrying four and more foci increased.
source: In red1∆ and rrp6-32 cells, in which degradation of DSR transcripts was compromised, foci became prominent, and the frequencies of cells carrying four and more foci increased (Figure 3F,G and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,B,C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3F, 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A, 2B, 2C.

claim: Foci in red1∆ and rrp6-32 cells colocalized with Mmi1 inside the nucleus.
source: These foci also colocalized with Mmi1 inside the nucleus (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D,E).
evidence: This is supported by colocalization data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2D, 2E.

claim: Mmi1 lacking the C-terminal YTH domain (Mmi1-∆YTH) showed similar localization to that of full-length Mmi1.
source: Mmi1 lacking the C-terminal YTH domain (Mmi1-∆YTH) showed similar localization to that of full-length Mmi1 (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4A, 4B.

claim: The domain of residues 61–180 of Mmi1 had the ability to form nuclear foci.
source: We then attempted to determine the region responsible for foci formation in the N-terminus of Mmi1, and found that the domain of residues 61–180 had the ability to form nuclear foci (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Mmi1 interacted with itself through the domain of residues 61–180.
source: Two-hybrid analyses and immunoprecipitation assays indicated that Mmi1 interacted with itself through this domain (Figure 4C,D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,C), so we designated this region SID (self-interaction domain).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4C, 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, 1C.

claim: The region of residues 61–180 of Mmi1 is designated SID (self-interaction domain).
source: Two-hybrid analyses and immunoprecipitation assays indicated that Mmi1 interacted with itself through this domain (Figure 4C,D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,C), so we designated this region SID (self-interaction domain).
evidence: This is a definition based on the experimental observation of self-interaction.

claim: Mmi1 lacking SID (Mmi1-∆SID) retained the ability to bind to the DSR region.
source: Mmi1 lacking SID (Mmi1-∆SID) retained the ability to bind to the DSR region (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by electrophoretic mobility shift assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Mmi1-∆SID lost the function to induce the elimination of DSR-containing transcripts.
source: However, Mmi1-∆SID lost the function to induce the elimination of DSR-containing transcripts (Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1E) and could not rescue the growth defect of temperature-sensitive mmi1 mutant cells (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4E, 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Mmi1-∆SID could not rescue the growth defect of temperature-sensitive mmi1 mutant cells.
source: However, Mmi1-∆SID lost the function to induce the elimination of DSR-containing transcripts (Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1E) and could not rescue the growth defect of temperature-sensitive mmi1 mutant cells (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Expression of Mmi1-∆YTH had a dominant-negative effect.
source: It was also noted that expression of Mmi1-∆YTH had a dominant-negative effect (Figure 4E,F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4E, 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Deletion of SID resulted in loss of interaction with Red1.
source: Deletion of SID also resulted in loss of interaction with Red1 (Figure 4G), suggesting that Mmi1 interacts with factors involved in Mmi1-mediated elimination through SID.
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Mmi1 interacts with factors involved in Mmi1-mediated elimination through SID.
source: Deletion of SID also resulted in loss of interaction with Red1 (Figure 4G), suggesting that Mmi1 interacts with factors involved in Mmi1-mediated elimination through SID.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that SID deletion abolishes Red1 interaction.

claim: mei4 and ssm4 transcripts were mainly observed in the cytoplasm of mmi1 mutant cells expressing Mmi1-∆SID.
source: mei4 and ssm4 transcripts were mainly observed in the cytoplasm of mmi1 mutant cells expressing Mmi1-∆SID, as cells expressing Mmi1-∆YTH (Figure 5A,B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by smFISH data shown in Figure 5A, 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, 1B.

claim: Nuclear foci of the reporter transcripts were dispersed in cells expressing Mmi1-∆SID.
source: Nuclear foci of the reporter transcripts were dispersed in cells expressing Mmi1-∆SID (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A,B), although full-length transcripts accumulated (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A, 2B, 2C.

claim: Full-length reporter transcripts accumulated in cells expressing Mmi1-∆SID.
source: Nuclear foci of the reporter transcripts were dispersed in cells expressing Mmi1-∆SID (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A,B), although full-length transcripts accumulated (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C.
